title: Implement Selection Sort — find the smallest element, put it first, then find next smallest, put it second, repeat; O(n²).

s1_definition.profdef: Selection sort is a comparison-based algorithm that divides the array into a sorted prefix and an unsorted suffix. On each pass it scans the unsorted suffix to find the minimum element and swaps it into the first unsorted position, growing the sorted prefix by one. It has quadratic time in all cases, constant extra space, and performs at most n minus one swaps, which is its distinguishing advantage. The basic version is not stable.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India lining up account balances from smallest to largest. The clerk scans the entire pile to find the single smallest balance and places it firmly at the front. Then she scans the remaining pile to find the next smallest and places it second. She repeats, each time selecting the minimum of what is left and locking it into the next position, until the whole line is sorted. The front of the line is always finished and never touched again.
s1_definition.oneliner: Selection sort repeatedly finds the smallest remaining element and swaps it into the next sorted position.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Selection sort is a comparison-based algorithm that divides the array into a sorted prefix and an unsorted suffix. On each pass it scans the unsorted suffix to find the minimum element and swaps it into the first unsorted position, growing the sorted prefix by one. It has quadratic time in all cases, constant extra space, and performs at most n minus one swaps, which is its distinguishing advantage. The basic version is not stable.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India lining up account balances from smallest to largest. The clerk scans the entire pile to find the single smallest balance and places it firmly at the front. Then she scans the remaining pile to find the next smallest and places it second. She repeats, each time selecting the minimum of what is left and locking it into the next position, until the whole line is sorted. The front of the line is always finished and never touched again.

**One line to remember:** Selection sort repeatedly finds the smallest remaining element and swaps it into the next sorted position.

sections.s2_technical:
Selection sort uses two nested loops. The outer loop marks the boundary between the sorted prefix and the unsorted suffix, advancing one position each pass. The inner loop scans the entire unsorted suffix to find the index of the minimum element.

Finding the minimum works by tracking the smallest-so-far index. We start with `int minIndex = i;` then scan with `if (arr[j].compareTo(arr[minIndex]) < 0) minIndex = j;` updating whenever we find something smaller. After the inner loop, we perform a single swap bringing that minimum to the front of the unsorted region with `swap(arr, i, minIndex);`.

The defining characteristic is the swap count. Unlike bubble sort which can swap many times per pass, selection sort does exactly one swap per pass, so at most n minus one swaps total. This matters when writes are expensive, for example on flash memory or when each element is large and copying is costly, because selection sort minimises writes even though it still does quadratic comparisons.

A senior-level point is that the basic selection sort is not stable, because the long-distance swap can jump an equal element past another, changing their relative order. It can be made stable by shifting instead of swapping, at the cost of more moves. Like bubble sort, its quadratic comparison count makes it unsuitable for large data, and I would not ship it. Its honest niches are tiny arrays and situations where the number of writes must be minimised. It is primarily a teaching algorithm that clearly separates the sorted and unsorted regions.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India wants to display a small leaderboard of the lowest account balances flagged for review, ordered from smallest to largest. Selection sort naturally builds the sorted order from the front by repeatedly picking the smallest remaining balance, which maps cleanly to "show the smallest first, then the next smallest".

Problem 2 — In this particular system the balance records are large objects that are expensive to move, so we want an algorithm that minimises the number of swaps even if it does many comparisons. Selection sort is ideal here because it performs at most one swap per pass, the fewest of the simple sorts.

In our mini-project we build a `SelectionSorter` that sorts an array of BigDecimal balances ascending, logging the minimum found and the swap on each pass. The demo sorts a small array of the bank's balances and shows the sorted prefix growing one element at a time.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: the array 300000, 50000, 1000000, 75000.

Step 1: Pass one scans the whole array for the minimum. The smallest is 50000 at index one. We swap it with index zero, giving 50000, 300000, 1000000, 75000. The sorted prefix is now just the first element.

Step 2: Pass two scans indices one through three. The minimum there is 75000 at index three. We swap it with index one, giving 50000, 75000, 1000000, 300000. The sorted prefix is now two elements.

Step 3: Pass three scans indices two and three. The minimum is 300000 at index three. We swap it with index two, giving 50000, 75000, 300000, 1000000. The sorted prefix is three elements.

Step 4: The outer loop stops after n minus one passes, since the final element must already be the largest. No pass is needed for it.

Step 5: Notice the total number of swaps was exactly three, one per pass, which is the hallmark of selection sort and far fewer than bubble sort would do.

Step 6: The final array is 50000, 75000, 300000, 1000000, sorted ascending in place.

```
[2026-10-26 20:45:02] INFO    Before: [300000, 50000, 1000000, 75000]
[2026-10-26 20:45:02] INFO    Pass 1: placed min 50000 (from index 1) at position 0 → [50000, 300000, 1000000, 75000]
[2026-10-26 20:45:02] INFO    Pass 2: placed min 75000 (from index 3) at position 1 → [50000, 75000, 1000000, 300000]
[2026-10-26 20:45:02] INFO    Pass 3: placed min 300000 (from index 3) at position 2 → [50000, 75000, 300000, 1000000]
[2026-10-26 20:45:02] INFO    After:  [50000, 75000, 300000, 1000000]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  [300000, 50000, 1000000, 75000]
    │ pass 1: find min=50000, swap to front
    ▼
  [50000 | 300000, 1000000, 75000]     sorted prefix = 1
    │ pass 2: find min=75000 in suffix
    ▼
  [50000, 75000 | 1000000, 300000]     sorted prefix = 2
    │ pass 3: find min=300000 in suffix
    ▼
  [50000, 75000, 300000 | 1000000]     sorted prefix = 3 → done
  Total swaps: 3 (one per pass)
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Selection Sort ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Select-minimum-then-swap: one swap per pass                  │
  │  Sorted-prefix/unsorted-suffix partition invariant            │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ───────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: SelectionSorter only sorts                               │
  │  O: comparator variant could generalise the ordering         │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ────────────────────────────────────────

  ┌───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │            SelectionSorter            │
  │  ──────────────────────────────────── │
  │  + sortAscending(arr): void           │  O(n²) compares, ≤n-1 swaps
  │  - swap(arr, i, j): void              │  O(1) space, not stable
  └───────────────────────────────────────┘
      invariant: arr[0..i-1] sorted and final

  ── Call Chain ────────────────────────────────────────────

  1. sortAscending(arr) → for each i, scan suffix for minIndex
  2. swap(i, minIndex) once
  3. sorted prefix grows by one each pass
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Selection sort divides the array into a sorted prefix and an unsorted suffix. On each pass it scans the entire unsorted suffix to find the minimum element and swaps that minimum into the first unsorted position, which grows the sorted prefix by one. It repeats until the whole array is sorted. It has quadratic time in every case, uses only constant extra memory, and the basic version is not stable.

The distinguishing feature I always highlight is the swap count. Selection sort performs exactly one swap per pass, so at most n minus one swaps in total, which is the fewest of all the simple sorts. That is its real advantage: when writes are expensive, for example on flash memory or when each element is a large object that is costly to move, selection sort minimises the number of moves even though it still does many comparisons.

In my banking context at the National Bank of India I used it conceptually for a small low-balance review leaderboard, ordering flagged accounts from smallest balance to largest, because selection sort builds the order from the front exactly as "show the smallest first, then the next smallest". In a system where the balance records were large and expensive to copy, the minimal-swap property was the reason to prefer it over bubble sort.

The senior-level honesty I offer is that its quadratic comparisons make it unsuitable for large datasets, so I would not ship it for general sorting. The basic version is also unstable because a long-distance swap can jump an equal element past another, though it can be made stable by shifting instead of swapping at the cost of more moves. Its genuine niches are tiny arrays and write-minimising scenarios, and otherwise it is a clear teaching algorithm that cleanly separates the sorted and unsorted regions. For real work I use the library sort.

keyPoints: Comparison sorts: merge sort O(n log n), quick sort O(n log n) average
Non-comparison: counting sort, radix sort — O(n) for limited range
Kth largest: quickselect O(n) average, heap O(n log k)
